claims.text: Applying an approximately 20 nm silver coating to tungsten particles by electroless plating before consolidation is the proposed intervention.
Inert-atmosphere sintering at approximately 1000 °C will produce good interfacial bonding while limiting interdiffusion.
The coating and consolidation process will form a continuous, nanostructured Ag interlayer at W–Cu interfaces.
The Ag interlayer will be robust under composite consolidation.
Silver has sufficiently high intrinsic thermal conductivity to enhance electron transport between tungsten and copper.
The Ag interlayer will reduce thermal boundary resistance at W–Cu interfaces.
The Ag interlayer will enhance electron–phonon energy transfer or coupling at the W–Cu interface.
The ductility of the Ag interlayer will support the mechanical integrity of the W–Cu composite during thermal cycling.
The Ag interlayer has sufficient irradiation resistance to preserve composite integrity under fusion-reactor irradiation.
Ag-coated tungsten particles will yield higher overall thermal conductivity than otherwise comparable uncoated-particle W–Cu composites.
The thermal-conductivity increase will occur without compromising mechanical durability.
The thermal-conductivity increase will occur without compromising irradiation resistance.
The proposed benefit requires processing that keeps the Ag interlayer stable by limiting interdiffusion.
The proposed benefit should persist under high thermal flux, irradiation, and thermal cycling representative of fusion-reactor joints.
Variations in Ag-layer uniformity and interdiffusion may alter the magnitude of the thermal-conductivity enhancement.
Current evidence supports the stability of the Ag interlayer under the optimized processing parameters.
